item.title: 7 Signs Your Therapist Might Not Be a Good Fit for You
item.description:
Therapy

7 Signs Your Therapist Might Not Be a Good Fit for You

From endless validation to unsolicited advice, signs to watch for in therapy.

Posted November 9, 2026

Key points
  • A therapist who agrees with everything you say may be validating you without helping you grow.
  • Good therapy goes beyond venting, offering insight into your patterns, relationships, and behaviors.
  • The right therapist welcomes feedback, respects boundaries, and helps you find your own answers.
Source: New Africa / Shutterstock

Finding the right therapist can feel a lot like dating. You browse through profiles, ask around, and then schedule an initial meeting, hoping there’s chemistry. Sometimes you click immediately, but other times, you have to wait for your therapist to grow on you.

Just like any other relationship, the therapeutic relationship is about finding the right match. Not every therapist is going to be a good fit for you. Just because someone has a degree, a cute office, and a comfy couch doesn’t necessarily mean they have the capacity to support your needs.

Therapy is an investment of your time, money, and emotional energy. You deserve to feel that the person sitting across from you is genuinely invested in understanding you and helping you grow.

Of course, good therapy isn’t always comfortable. In fact, the most meaningful sessions are often the ones that leave you a little confused and a little raw. Questioning your assumptions, confronting your beliefs, and recognizing patterns are non-negotiable aspects of successful therapy.

But there’s a difference between being challenged in therapy and feeling that your therapist isn’t meeting your needs.

Here are seven signs your therapist might not be the right fit.

1. They agree with everything you say.

If your therapist thinks you’re always right, all your exes are narcissists, and everyone in your family is toxic, you may have hired a very expensive cheerleader.

A good therapist will validate your feelings, but they’ll also, in the nicest possible way, confront you and challenge your assumptions.

Ask yourself if your therapist invites you to consider another perspective and helps you confront how your own fears, expectations, and behaviors contribute to your experiences rather than just validating you.

2. They keep missing the plot.

You’ve spent three sessions talking about how your sister wasn’t invited to your wedding because she had an affair with your fiancé. And the next week, your therapist asks, “So, how are things with your sister? Have you two been spending time together?”

Therapists don’t need photographic memories. We’re human, and we talk to a lot of people. But it’s our responsibility to find ways to remember important patterns, relationships, and events in someone’s life so we can help them build awareness and make connections.

When a therapist repeatedly forgets significant details, you may find yourself feeling betrayed and spending session time reiterating the same stories. Also, paying attention to your story is a part of helping you feel seen. It’s challenging to develop trust when you feel dismissed, which is inevitable when someone who is paid to pay attention to you doesn't.

3. Every session feels like a very expensive coffee date.

You chat, you laugh, you catch up, but the conversations don’t lead anywhere.

You discuss your weekend, complain about your boss, recap your latest dating disaster, and suddenly your 50 minutes are up. See you next Tuesday!

Therapy isn’t always about measurable progress, and chitchat is part of relationship building, but there should be some sense of direction, insight, and exploration that your sessions build on.

Seemingly ordinary conversations can allow us to make significant discoveries. A conversation about a disagreement with a roommate might open the door to exploring your discomfort with conflict or your tendency to prioritize everyone else’s needs.

You don’t need a life-changing revelation every week, but over time, therapy should offer more than an opportunity to vent.

4. They diagnose everyone in your life.

Your mother is histrionic. Your dad is a workaholic. Your boyfriend is avoidant. Apparently, you’re the only psychologically healthy person in your world.

A good therapist helps you understand relational dynamics, identify your own role in them, and empowers you to make changes, rather than handing out diagnoses to people they’ve never met.

It’s tempting to explain difficult relationships by attaching psychological labels to the people involved. However, your therapist’s job is to recognize problematic behaviors, not assign a clinical diagnosis based on someone else’s account.

The goal of therapy should be to guide you to understand your relationships, empower you, and help you develop healthier ways of navigating them.

5. They make your therapy about themselves.

You’re reaching for tissues as you tell your therapist about a painful breakup, and suddenly you’re hearing a 15-minute story about their divorce.

Appropriate self-disclosure can be useful, but if you’re learning more about your therapist than yourself, something isn’t right.

Therapists are people, too. We have families, hobbies, favorite books, and experiences that sometimes overlap with those of our clients. Sharing a personal anecdote can help normalize an experience, strengthen connection, or reduce isolation. However, if you regularly find yourself listening to your therapist’s problems, comforting them, or wondering how to redirect the conversation back to yourself, the boundaries may have become blurred.

6. They can’t tolerate being challenged by you.

You tell them something they said didn’t sit right with you, and suddenly they’re more defensive than your ex.

A good therapist can acknowledge mistakes, welcome feedback, and work through ruptures in the therapeutic relationship.

Your therapist, who is also human, may make inaccurate assumptions, forget a session, or approach a sensitive topic a little too abruptly. Human error is inevitable in any meaningful relationship, including therapy. Misunderstandings in therapy may serve as an opportunity for you to voice your needs and boundaries. If your therapist is able to respond with accountability, that might serve as a corrective experience and may even strengthen the therapeutic alliance.

In contrast, a therapist who becomes dismissive, defensive, or makes you feel guilty for expressing your concerns may unintentionally reinforce the very relational patterns you’re trying to change.

7. They give you advice instead of helping you find your own answers.

A good therapist isn’t there to make your decisions for you. They should help you understand what’s driving your choices, explore your options, and develop the confidence to make decisions that are right for you.

Of course, therapists can offer guidance, practical suggestions, and recommendations when appropriate. Therapy is about helping someone evaluate their choices, not telling them how to live.

For example, you might already know that your boyfriend is letting you down. What you may not understand is why leaving him feels impossible or why being alone feels more frightening than being with someone who is not all that nice to you. Good therapy helps you develop the insight and emotional capacity to make your own decisions, even when those decisions are difficult.

Finding the right therapist

Your therapist doesn’t need to be your best friend, your personal cheerleader, or your life coach. They should be someone who helps you see what you might not want to see while creating an environment where you feel safe enough to explore it.

And remember, a therapist can be perfectly competent and still not be the right fit for you.

Different therapists have different personalities, approaches, and areas of expertise. Some are more structured and directive, while others are more exploratory. Some employ humor and use themselves as a part of the process, while others are a little more distant and leave more room for reflection. What works beautifully for one person may feel unhelpful to another.

Many therapists offer complimentary consultation sessions for you to ask them questions and assess fit. Don’t feel like you have to commit to the first therapist you meet.

Therapy asks you to be vulnerable, honest, and willing to examine parts of yourself you may have spent years avoiding. Finding someone you can trust with that process is an important piece.

To find a therapist near you, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: Why Do I Go Numb Instead of Feeling Things?
item.description:
Emotions

Why Do I Go Numb Instead of Feeling Things?

Emotional numbness can keep us moving—and hide how much we care.

Posted November 9, 2026

Key points
  • Emotional numbness can soften disappointment while making it harder to remember how much something mattered.
  • Messages about masculinity can teach men to move on from experiences without acknowledging our feelings.
  • Getting curious about numbness, rather than forcing a feeling, can create room to recognize what mattered.

I was an actor in New York. Yes, that’s right—I didn’t emerge from the womb asking people how they felt for a living. I had dreams of being on Broadway, and after years of work, I finally got invited to the final callbacks for the lead role in a Broadway musical. For this final audition, I was going to wear my grandfather’s vintage pinstriped suit. I planned on changing into it at the audition studio to make sure it looked crisp. But while walking down 43rd Street, half a block from the audition, the suit fell out of my hands and into a pile of Central Park carriage horse manure. Terrified that I’d smell up the room and ruin my chances at the role, I rushed to the bathroom and tried to scrub out the stains before putting the suit on and walking into the audition.

Suffice it to say, I didn’t get the part. I got some generic feedback about how I didn’t have the right look. But I don’t really remember much of that part—the days and weeks afterward are a blank spot in my memory. And while I can recall the moment I dropped that suit on 43rd Street like it was yesterday, I can’t remember how I felt about not landing my big Broadway break. I can barely remember finding out I didn’t get it. The whole experience is a fog, as if the details and the feelings attached to them have been swallowed up together. When I reach back and try to remember how I felt about losing out on this role, the only thing I feel is... nothing.

What is emotional numbing?

Emotional numbing is a sense of being disconnected from your feelings. You might have a sense that something matters to you but not be able to feel much about it. Sometimes we disconnect like this in response to stress that threatens to overwhelm us. If we feel less, we can keep moving forward.

I see this often in work with clients—when moving towards a memory that holds a lot of charge, they’ll often just go blank, fuzz out, or suddenly be unable to recall details. I think of it like the villain from that ’80s movie, The NeverEnding Story: the Nothing. If you’re not an ’80s kid like me, the Nothing threatens to consume the magical land of Fantasia. It grows as people lose their hopes and forget their dreams. That’s the image that comes up for me when I try to describe my experience of it. I start to feel the big feeling coming on. Sometimes I even experience it for a moment. But as it threatens to overwhelm me, the Nothing swoops in so that I can move on.

While I invented my own ’80s fanboy name for what I’m experiencing, researchers have been exploring this topic for some time. There’s a related experience called alexithymia, which is difficulty identifying and describing our own emotions. Imagine being asked how you feel about a certain topic, reaching into wherever emotions live in us, and just hitting a wall. From the inside, it can be really hard to distinguish between “I don’t know how I feel” and “I don’t feel anything.”

Why do men go emotionally numb?

Emotional numbness isn’t unique to men, but we do seem to have a corner on the market. And that makes sense given the messages we receive about what is and isn’t acceptable to feel. Psychologist Ronald Levant uses the term normative male alexithymia to describe a pattern found in many men who experience difficulty identifying and expressing emotion—particularly those emotions tied to vulnerability or intimacy. He believes this pattern is rooted in the way men are socialized in our society.

Those of us raised as men learn these messages early and often. We inherit them and gift them to each other: “Don’t cry. Don’t be so sensitive. Don’t let them see you care.” I honestly can’t remember where I first received this message. I’m tempted to chalk that one up to the Nothing, too.

But my Nothing isn’t a villain from a kids movie. I think of him as a part of me that learned to perform a job. And he performs it very well. I suspect the Nothing is the reason I’ve been able to succeed at grad school, to switch careers, to build a private practice. But the Nothing doesn’t discriminate between the pain of the story and the importance of the story itself: A friendship ends, and we convince ourselves it wasn’t that important anyway. A dream falls to manure (literally), and we find something else to want.

In my experience, the Nothing doesn’t just take away the disappointment. It also makes it harder to remember how much we cared. I wish that I could have given myself the time to really feel the disappointment and the sadness of seeing my dream slip through my fingers. My experience feels incomplete in my mind, like a book without the final chapter.

What helps when you feel emotionally numb?

Sometimes in the middle of a session, a client goes blank. It’s not like they fully check out of the room, but they’ll be dipping their toe into an emotion and then just lose connection with it. When that happens, I’ll often invite them to notice what happens as they get closer to it. And sometimes they can’t. Sometimes the details are fuzzy, or there’s simply nothing there, and they get frustrated. That’s okay.

Noticing we can’t connect is a good place to start. Sometimes that blankness is doing a job, too. Rather than forcing our way through it, we can get curious about what feeling it might be protecting. And maybe, just maybe, that curiosity gives way to a name: sorrow, regret, grief. The point isn’t to choose the emotion we think we’re supposed to have. It’s to explore if we can connect with even the faintest sense of “Yes, that’s it.”

I think about younger me walking down 43rd Street with my grandfather’s suit, so excited and scared about what might happen next. I wish I could go back and tell him: “I see how much this matters to you. Whether you get the role or not, I want you to remember how much this matters. Don’t let that be taken from you.” We don’t have to convince ourselves a dream didn’t matter just because it didn’t come true. Sometimes, nearly 20 years later, we can give ourselves the chance to write about it and remember that it mattered.

item.title: Elizabeth Holmes Almost Fooled Me. I'm a Psychiatrist.
item.description:
Deception

Elizabeth Holmes Almost Fooled Me. I'm a Psychiatrist.

While watching the new documentary, her naïveté made me question the truth.

Posted November 9, 2026

Key points
  • Apparent naïveté can weaken skepticism even when evidence of fraud is overwhelming.
  • Sympathy can lead us to reinterpret evidence to resolve conflicts between emotion and reason.
  • Even expertise in human behavior offers no immunity to emotionally persuasive narratives.

I've spent decades studying human behavior and the brain and always felt I had a knack for spotting liars. But while watching You Can See Everything, Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim's documentary about Elizabeth Holmes, I found myself momentarily wondering whether, despite her criminal conviction, she might be telling the truth.

It wasn't her tears that persuaded me. Those seemed theatrical, in my opinion. Nor was it her need to interrupt an interview to rush and check on her baby, just before her partner, Billy Evans, raised the possibility of financial compensation from the film. Grandiosity, self-importance, fixation on success, and other traits that Holmes reveals are typical of narcissism, but those behavioral observations are not a diagnosis, and these personality traits alone cannot explain her actions.

Seeming Naïveté

What almost hooked me was her apparent naïveté. Holmes seemed genuinely bewildered by Abbott and Costello's famous "Who's on First?" routine and portrayed herself as uninterested in financial matters. Could this extraordinarily ambitious woman, who attended Stanford and built a multibillion-dollar company, really be so socially awkward and financially unsophisticated?

Some have speculated that Holmes might be on the autism spectrum, and I wondered that as well, though such observations are by no means a clinical assessment. Her behavior may have reflected an unusual way of processing social information rather than an attempt to evade responsibility, but these were fleeting impressions. As soon as a scene ended, my analytical mind jumped in and reminded me of the overwhelming evidence of her deception. For a moment, however, I had suspended my skepticism. The film doesn't just show us how a persuasive individual can deceive people, but it draws us in, questioning her veracity, even when we know better.

I kept wondering how someone as devious as Holmes could persuade smart people who know better to overlook piles of evidence against her. She convinced Henry Kissinger, George Shultz, and other highly accomplished individuals to lend their reputations to Theranos, her so-called miracle company. How could they have been so thoroughly misled?

It may come down to how our brains reconcile emotion and reason. We know that Holmes was convicted of fraud, but when we observe her apparent vulnerability, it is tempting to believe her. To relieve this cognitive dissonance, we may search for explanations. Maybe she really is socially awkward and was manipulated by the men in her life. The more we sympathize with Holmes, the more tempting it becomes to reinterpret the evidence against her.

Faulty Memory

In clinical practice, I've encountered people whose accounts of events become increasingly fixed through repetition, particularly when those accounts protect a valued self-image. Over time, people may come to believe their own distorted versions of events.

Holmes repeatedly responds to difficult questions by claiming she doesn't remember, and some of her responses seem remarkably convincing. But after spending much of my career studying memory, I know that our recollections can be far less reliable than we imagine.

Memory isn't a video recording that we can replay. Each time we recall a memory, there is the potential to distort it by incorporating new information, feelings, and interpretations based on subsequent experiences. After repeatedly recounting an event, those distortions may feel authentic. This vulnerability is shared by all of us; it’s not just a feature of any personality type.

Consider former NBC News anchor Brian Williams, who repeatedly recounted being aboard a helicopter struck by enemy fire during the Iraq War. When his account was challenged, he acknowledged that he had been in a different helicopter and attributed the discrepancy to conflated memories. The controversy cost him his job as the evening news anchor.

When Holmes insists that she doesn't remember something, we know from her past behavior that she is likely lying. But it is possible that she may be repeating a version of reality that she has come to believe.

The Men in Her Life

Holmes's relationships with the men in her life bring up another question about who is in control. During her trial, Holmes described her former romantic and business partner, Sunny Balwani, as controlling and abusive. Her allegations were disputed, and they did not prevent her conviction. Now we watch Evans, her current partner, become an increasingly forceful defender of her narrative.

When the filmmakers return to Evans after an extended interval, I was struck by how his demeanor became more combative and suspicious. Was he protecting someone he believes has been unjustly treated? Has he become so invested in her version of events that he can no longer see disputing evidence or even question it? Or, maybe, Holmes is presenting herself as a woman controlled by powerful men, when actually she may be the one pulling the strings, leaving the men to shoulder responsibility for her actions. It's hard to tell who's really controlling whom.

Emotions and Judgment

Fielder and Oppenheim seem to understand how easily our emotions can influence our judgment. Holmes once offered investors an irresistible story about transforming medicine. Now she presents another: a misunderstood visionary, perhaps socially awkward, perhaps manipulated by others, and ultimately victimized by forces beyond her control.

Whether she consciously constructed that persona or has even come to believe parts of it herself is impossible to know. I began watching the film confident in my ability to recognize deception. I finished with a reminder of how easily even a psychiatrist's skepticism can falter.

For me, the most unsettling thing about Elizabeth Holmes wasn’t simply her ability to make us believe her. It was her ability to make me want to believe her. The most effective deception doesn't always overcome our intelligence. Sometimes it enlists our empathy.

item.title: When Your Sense of Familiarity Falls Apart
item.description:
Capgras Syndrome

When Your Sense of Familiarity Falls Apart

Capgras syndrome can make someone believe a familiar person is an impostor.

Posted November 9, 2026

Key points
  • The TV series “Phony” introduces a puzzling question about perception that could point to Capgras syndrome.
  • Capgras syndrome can make familiar people, pets, or objects seem like impostors.
  • Capgras can occur after head trauma or alongside dementia, Alzheimer’s disease, or schizophrenia.
A silver tabby cat sees a reflection of itself which represents what Jane interprets as an imposter after her accident.
Source: Chat GPT AI

“Phony,” the new television series streaming on several networks, follows a plot closely tied to a neurological condition. Sonny, after waking up from a car accident, perceives that his mother is a phony. He believes she is not his true mother. This, of course, puts this young man in a spin. The question is, what happened that led to Sonny’s uncomfortable feelings about his mother?

Among several conditions that could explain this phenomenon, Capgras syndrome is a strong contender. As a neurologist, I’ve written about it and included it in lectures about collecting. The logic is that if the art piece we purchase is a “phony,” we collectors value it less. This has parallels to Sonny’s feelings for his mother in the movie after his car accident.

An Example of Capgras Syndrome

Whatever the cause, the afflicted individual can misinterpret not only people previously close to them as fake, but also pets and even inanimate objects. For example (hypothetical): Jane has a favorite cat called Ernie. He sleeps on the dining room table in the sun when she is not home and begs for food at the same table when she dines. Though these habits of Jane’s cat may seem repugnant to some, they suit Jane just fine.

But things changed after her bike accident. She was in a coma for three days and then had to go to rehabilitation therapy for several months to regain her cognitive skills. When she returned home, she insisted Ernie was not Ernie. She claimed the cat, who had the same preferences as before Jane’s accident, was not him, even though she felt she was the same. Jane said Ernie might look like and act like her old feline, but he was an impostor.

The Origin of Capgras Syndrome

This is the known explanation. Due to faulty brain wiring after a car accident or head trauma, or dementia/Alzheimer’s disease or schizophrenia, delusions can surface, suggesting Capgras syndrome. Emotional distress can be another contributor, plus other medical conditions have been reported as being associated with it.

Conclusion

So, was Sonny afflicted by Capgras syndrome? I’ll leave the reader to enjoy the television series and decide.

In the meantime, we collectors have to use every tool possible to avoid fakes, which collectors are likely to devalue compared to authentic pieces. According to Artnet News, over 50 percent of art on the market is forged or misattributed. In other words, phony.

item.title: Curiosity: The Most Underused Clinical Tool
item.description:
Integrative Medicine

Curiosity: The Most Underused Clinical Tool

Engaging curiosity holds our first impression lightly enough to investigate it.

Posted November 9, 2026

Key points
  • Curiosity allows healthcare providers to uncover what the initial assessment may have left out.
  • There are moments during an ordinary patient visit when a simple question can help redirect the work.
  • If responses challenge initial assumptions, providers need to be willing to change the plan of action.

Imagine a patient who works as a delivery driver. After a couple of months, the patient returns for a follow-up appointment with blood pressure that remains above the goal the physician set. The physician prescribed the appropriate daily medication, covered how to take it, and confirmed understanding. Despite this, the patient reports only taking the medication a few times a week. What the physician doesn’t know is that the medication increases trips to the bathroom and interferes with his tight delivery schedule.

What often happens in these scenarios? The healthcare provider spends the next several minutes of the appointment reiterating why taking the medication as prescribed is important, crucial even, for lowering blood pressure and all the risks associated with not taking it correctly. Before going through that conversation, another question worth asking may have saved both a lot of time: “Can you walk me through what happens on the days you don’t take your medication?” or “How are the days you don’t take medication different from the ones when you take your medication?” The answer can significantly change the conversation and provide the clinician with information tied to a particular issue or set of issues that can be addressed, while just another conversation about why it is important to take the medication as prescribed would have left the problem unaddressed.

Questions like these hold a spark of curiosity that allow the healthcare provider to get into the contextual layers of patients’ lives and uncover what the initial assessment may have left out. This is why curiosity deserves more attention as a legitimate clinical tool.

When an Explanation Becomes an Assumption

With experience, clinicians learn to recognize and identify patterns that help them interpret symptoms, anticipate potential complications, and develop evidence-based treatment plans. This is how medical students have been learning and how researchers and clinicians have been advancing treatment options for years. This is also how AI comes into play, through its processing power. The risk of relying solely on pattern recognition, without questioning and without curiosity, is becoming so comfortable with familiar patterns that we stop asking whether it fits the person across from us.

It becomes easy to interpret a missed appointment as a lack of commitment, or to read medication hesitation as resistance or failure to change a pattern, or even see unhealthy eating habits as a lack of motivation. The descriptor seems plausible, particularly when it feels like the pattern has been seen before. However, it is critical to remember that plausibility and confirmation are not the same thing.

Consider for a moment another patient, one who hasn’t scheduled a recommended evaluation. There are several potential explanations. Maybe transportation is an obstacle, or their work schedule is prohibitive. The patient might be terrified that the evaluation will confirm they have an illness that took their parent’s life. Each situation calls for a different conversation and different types of support.

Engaging curiosity asks us to hold our first impression lightly enough to investigate it. We need to be ready to ask questions aimed at understanding:

  • What does the patient understand about the recommendation I just made?
  • What do they expect will happen if they follow through?
  • What have they already tried?
  • What are they afraid of saying in that moment?

The answers we receive may challenge our initial assumptions, and we need to be ready and willing to change the plan of action when they do.

Understanding Has to Change the Care

In a 2013 article in the Annals of Internal Medicine, Weiner and colleagues conducted an observational study exploring how adapting care to a patient’s circumstances affected treatment outcomes. They found that when physicians asked the right questions, or gave room for patients to share context information, the problems the patient came in to address were significantly more likely to improve. Findings such as these highlight the importance of curiosity and using what we learn about patients’ lives to shape the care we provide.

So, for that patient working as a delivery driver, what would that look like? It could mean reviewing medication concerns and discussing medically appropriate prescription options that fit with his day-to-day responsibilities. For another patient who simply cannot afford the prescription, it could mean finding a more affordable alternative. And for someone who fears medical tests, it could mean creating space for the patient to understand and explain their fear and providing resources and support on how to move forward.

A thoughtful, curiosity-driven question is the starting point of this work. Its value will depend on what happens after the answer.

Where Behavioral Health Contributes

Including psychologists in the process can help care teams turn curiosity into a more holistic understanding of the patient. Psychologists’ training emphasizes examining how beliefs, emotions, habits, relationships, and their daily lived experience shape behavior. When a patient struggles with a treatment plan, that expertise can help the team move beyond initial impressions to investigate the factors making the plan difficult to follow.

In integrated care environments, this may mean taking time to explore a fear the patient has not yet expressed, understanding factors reinforcing a longstanding habit, or identifying where a prescribed routine fails to align with the realities of a patient’s daily responsibilities. Working alongside the patient as part of the care team, the psychologist translates that understanding into a care plan that properly fits the patient’s daily life.

Making Room for the Answer

Of course, appointments are usually short, good documentation takes time, and when an open question is asked, we risk revealing problems requiring more help than a single visit can provide. The care team is also often already stretched thin, with little time and too much to do.

These challenges are real. Curiosity isn’t going to solve the staff problem a clinic faces; it also won’t help create affordable housing, provide a replacement for lost insurance, or create healthier and more accessible food and exercise options everywhere.

Still, there are moments during an ordinary visit when a simple question can help redirect the work. “What about this plan has been hardest for you? “What concerns do you have about this treatment plan?” “Is this a plan you feel can fit in and work with your typical day?” Being curious and asking a few open-ended questions can help a patient feel seen, feel more part of the treatment process, and lead to better outcomes.

Before explaining, again, why a patient should follow a prescribed treatment plan, be curious and investigate what is making the plan difficult to follow.

item.title: Sometimes You Need to Travel to See Your Life Clearly
item.description:
Divorce

Sometimes You Need to Travel to See Your Life Clearly

Personal Perspective: How a $500 plane ticket showed me a new possible future.

Posted November 9, 2026

Key points
  • The future isn't a single destination.
  • Sometimes you need new information, not a better plan.
  • Leaving familiar surroundings can expose life expectations you've mistaken for facts.

My financial advisor’s corner office literally hovered above Seattle’s Lake Union. A bald eagle soared past the window. I wondered what it would be like to work in a room with a window—never mind a view.

“Let’s look at your numbers,” she said.

“Let’s do it,” I agreed.

I was in the middle of a divorce, and a friend had insisted I see her financial planner to get my financial bearings. I took a deep breath, ready to be obedient to whatever plan this woman would lay out for me. The fear I’d been waking up with every day was killing me—fear about paying my rent, my student loan, my car payment, my credit card debt, my health insurance. I also had fear about the future and fear of digging out of my past.

I sat up straight and pulled my baseball cap back on my head. Ready.

She paused and then said, “If you want to retire at age 67 and live at the same standard of living you have now..."

My current standard of living wasn’t anything to write home about. I thought to myself, You mean living in a dingy little apartment with rats in the backyard and a dishwasher falling out of the wall. But I just waited.

She cleared her throat. “You’re going to need to save $12,000 per month between now and then.”

I suddenly couldn’t breathe. “How much?” I finally asked.

“Twelve thousand,” she repeated.

“Every month?”

“Yep,” she said.

“For the next 17 years?”

“Yep.”

Now I flat-out just stared at her until we were both uncomfortable.

She could feel my panic.

I gave her my credit card to pay her the $1,000 we’d agreed on for her advice, and gathered my things. We shook hands. I left the building, got into my half-paid-off Kia Soul and drove myself "home."

When I got there, I plopped myself down on the sofa that a friend had donated to me when she found out I was getting divorced.

I poured myself a glass of wine and cried. Then I opened my computer to look at my savings account. I had $831.26. I had a sudden urge to escape the reality of my life.

Still crying, I pulled up Expedia to see how I could get out of town for what I had in my account. If I could never retire, I might as well get out of dodge for a week now. There were cheap tickets to Panama City. I booked a round-trip airplane ticket for $492 and posted a note on social media. Did anyone know anyone I could stay with in Panama?

Source: Rustiness/Unsplash

When I got to Panama, I stayed in a hostel for a few nights and wandered through Casco Viejo, the city's historic district. I visited the Panama Canal, marveling at the audacity of it.

Then I traveled up through David and eventually made my way to Boquete, a mountain town filled with expats surrounded by lush green hills.

There I stayed with Diane, the friend of a friend—an 82-year-old retired US citizen who was living permanently in Panama, enjoying a life that seemed rich in all the ways that mattered. She had a condo, a community, adventure, beauty, and enough money to live comfortably. She even had a new boyfriend.

One evening over dinner, Diane said something amazing to me. “You know what? There are a lot of ways to live a life. You can make up different rules if you want. Look at me? I’m living on less than I get from my Social Security checks.”

That’s when I had my epiphany: Other people’s stories—even the stories our whole culture buys into—are just stories. I didn’t have to let the word “retirement” or any other word intimidate me. I could dream outside the box.

We all carry around ideas about how life is supposed to work. And these expectations become so deeply embedded that we stop recognizing them as assumptions. We mistake them for facts.

When our lives don't measure up, we get anxious or conclude we've failed.

In Panama, I started to understand that there were many ways to build a satisfying life. Some involved more money. Others might require moving halfway around the world.

I came home knowing that I had options.

And that changed everything.

By the time I boarded the plane to go back to my crappy apartment, I could see possibilities for my future that had been invisible to me before.

Of course, you don't have to leave the country to change your perspective. You could read a book, take a class, or have a conversation with someone whose life looks different from yours.

But there is something extra powerful about physically removing oneself from familiar surroundings.

However we do it, when we become strangers in a new place, we can see the world differently.

Two Things I Learned From That Trip

1. The future isn't a single destination.

When someone tells you what your future must look like, remember that they're working from their own assumptions—not from yours.

2. Sometimes you need new information, not a better plan.

I could have gone home from the financial planner's office and spent months trying to figure out how to earn enough money to meet her recommendation. Instead, I went somewhere that exposed me to an entirely different way of thinking about what I needed.

I've thought about that trip many times over the years because it gave me back a sense of possibility during a really scary time in my life.

That's what I think a “second wind” really is.

It's not necessarily a dramatic reinvention. Sometimes it's just a moment in time when you realize that the life you've been imagining isn't the only life available to you.

If you're feeling stuck, if the “numbers” don't add up, or if the future you've been told to prepare for feels impossible, consider this: You may not need to figure everything out all at once. You just might need a fresh perspective.

item.title: Which One Is the Real You?
item.description:
Relationships

Which One Is the Real You?

How relationships shape the many versions of ourselves.

Posted November 9, 2026

Key points
  • There is no single, fixed self. Relationships shape different versions of who we are.
  • Our social, tribal, and personal selves each serve different purposes.
  • How we feel about someone may depend partly on who we become in their presence.
  • We can approach our many selves with curiosity and compassion, nurturing those we value.

At work, you are known to be a serious, efficient, and decisive manager. When you are with your old high school friend, you become the comedian and social connector, leading karaoke dances, and cracking jokes. On a first date, understandably, you are a bit nervous, carefully choosing your words and may be a little too agreeable.

Challenging the Notion of a "True Self"

Which one is the real you?

We tend to assume that somewhere beneath these different personalities, there is a single true self. The others are performances, adaptations, or masks that we put on.

But what if that assumption is wrong?

What if all these versions of ourselves are real?

No one can be exactly the same person in every social situation. In fact, failing to consider the situation and the people around us may be selfish or even destructive, argues Japanese novelist Keiichiro Hirano in his book What Is the Self? From Individuals to Dividuals (my translation of the Japanese title).

His idea is simple on the surface: There is no “one” self. We are an aggregate of many selves” – Hirano calls this “dividuals” – a play on the word individual, suggesting that we are, after all, divisible. This is not a reference to dissociative identity disorder, but to the different selves that emerge through our relationships.

Many Versions of Ourselves Inside Us
Source: andrenawrski-Pixabay

As a neurologist, I have become increasingly skeptical of the idea that there is a single, fixed self, hidden somewhere deep inside our brains. Our thoughts, emotions, and behaviors emerge from dynamic interactions among multiple neural systems, constantly responding to our internal states and the world around us.

From this perspective, it seems unlikely that our sense of self would remain entirely unchanged across different situations and relationships. The part of us that wants to help a friend move and the part that wants to spend Saturday on the couch are both real.

Hirano describes three forms of dividuals that emerge through our relationships. With strangers, we may express a generic social dividual—a polite, socially appropriate version of ourselves. Within groups, such as workplaces, communities, or circles of friends, we develop tribal dividuals shaped by shared identities and expectations. In closer relationships, more personalized dividuals emerge, allowing us to reveal intimate aspects of ourselves. None is necessarily better or worse than the others. Each serves a different purpose.

Understanding Dividualism: Not Just Wearing Masks

One of the most important ideas in dividualism is that our different selves are not necessarily masks concealing a hidden, authentic self. Rather, they are constantly changing, shaped and reshaped through our interactions with others. Our memories, values, and experiences may provide some continuity, but no single dividual needs to represent our entire identity.

Hirano takes the reciprocal nature of relationships one step further. Our feelings toward another person may depend not only on who that person is, but also on who we become in their presence. We may enjoy spending time with a friend because we like the person we become around them—perhaps more relaxed, generous, or playful. Conversely, suppose my friend David disapproves of my new girlfriend, Mary. I may begin to resent David or feel guilty about disappointing him. Over time, I may avoid David not only because of his disapproval but also because I dislike the resentful, uncomfortable version of myself that emerges in our friendship.

When we have a crush, we desperately want to have that person like us. We may try to be funny, smart, charming, and may try to do something nice. But as we all know too well, relationships have this elusive “chemistry” aspect to them, and dividualism may help explain why that is. In relationships, not only there is another person at the end, but there is also our dividual – our own with the other person. Perhaps part of what we call "chemistry" is not simply liking another person but liking who we become together.

And when a relationship ends, we may mourn not only the loss of that person but also the version of ourselves that existed with them. When a parent dies, we may lose the only person with whom we still felt like a child. When a long career ends, we may miss not only the work but also the version of ourselves that existed among our colleagues. Perhaps this is part of what we mean when we say, "I feel as though I've lost a part of myself."

Over the course of our lives, some dividuals fade as relationships change or end, while others grow and flourish. Some lie dormant for years, only to reappear unexpectedly. Some reveal qualities we admire, while others expose parts of ourselves we would rather not see.

Choosing Which Selves to Nurture

Perhaps the question is not, "Which one is the real me?" but "Which versions of myself do I want to nurture?"

We do not need to love every version of ourselves, nor excuse every action. But perhaps recognizing that no single version defines us will allow us to approach our many selves with greater curiosity and compassion.

item.title: Downsizing Isn’t for Everyone
item.description:
Aging

Downsizing Isn’t for Everyone

Considering the personal and practical benefits of our possessions.

Posted November 9, 2026

Key points
  • We should not feel obligated to shed our belongings just to make it easier for our children.
  • Possessions can provide support for the future, cultivating a sense of aging in place.
  • For managing our belongings, there isn’t one fixed strategy across individuals or within an individual.
  • Most of us want to downsize as we get older—in a way that fits our own needs at our own pace.

As we grow older, we face considerable pressure to reduce our possessions and our living space. Such downsizing can have practical benefits and be personally liberating, but it can also lead to unnecessary stress and guilt.

This post does not criticize the act of downsizing, but it does push back against the pressure to do so, especially for the sake of our children. We can declutter and live more simply, but we should not feel obligated or guilted into discarding what is valuable to us.1

The Pressure to Downsize

Source: RDNE Stock Project/Pexels

Downsizing is often promoted as a virtuous gift and a way of showing love to our heirs. As middle-aged and elderly adults, we are counseled to reduce clutter so our children won’t face the arduous task of clearing out and cleaning after we die. We are also advised not to accumulate any new things because of the additional burden this will add.2

In an enlightening post on Swedish Death Cleaning, Psychology Today blogger Dr. Donelle Dreese offers a different perspective, saying that such cleaning “is an act of love for all those who will be in the position to clean out our ‘stuff’ after we are gone.”

Disciplined downsizing is also presented as a path to wisdom. By going through all of our possessions, seriously considering what matters to us and discarding the rest, we may move toward a deeper understanding of our place on Earth, “growing downward, smaller, one among the grasses,” in the words of poet Wendell Berry. Such downsizing conveys a moral imperative to acquire wisdom through un-acquiring possessions.

Gently Resisting the Pressure to Downsize

Source: Cottonbro Studio/Pexels

Considering the Children. For many of us, when we die, our children will be in middle age. The ideas in Swedish death cleaning and in KonMari about being a good ancestor are thoughtful and inspiring, but we are not in the best position to examine each of our possessions and determine its future personal value for others or its potential to give joy. Our middle-aged children will be quite capable of assessing what is or is not valuable to them.

In fact, grown children may discover interesting artifacts that tell them more about their parents. My father, for example, kept a file of published cartoons that my sister and I had never seen, left over from his young adulthood as an amateur cartoonist.

Source: Yan Krukau/Pexels

Considering Ourselves. If the things we own give us joy and pleasure, why not keep them? Our possessions are not disposable content.

I have small, unnecessary collections of first editions of poetry and memoir, which I enjoy seeing as I walk past them on the bookshelf, occasionally taking down one of the books and slowly reading.

And if something new comes along that delights us, then why not consider getting it?

Nurturing Future Generations. For many older adults, extra living space bestows hope that our grandchildren and grown children will visit and need guest rooms. Two of my grandchildren are now old enough to visit on their own—which they have done—and my extra bedrooms set up a more inviting environment.

Source: Isaac Quesada/Pexels

What Does the Research Say?

In general, as we grow older, we want autonomy with our belongings and living spaces. According to the AARP, nearly 90 percent of adults over 65 want to age in place whenever possible, in their current homes and with their own belongings.

Preserving Our Past. A pioneering study by Margaret Boschetti documented that cherished possessions contribute to our self concepts about who we are and what we’ve done. They help us remember important experiences, relationships, and identities of the past.

Looking Around and Looking Ahead. In a 2020 study, Tara Coleman and Janine Wiles found connections with belongings that transcend the past. The majority of participants in this study interacted with cherished possessions not only to connect with their past selves but also to cope with times of challenge and change in the present and to cultivate a sense of aging in place in the future.

Individual Differences. Research conducted by Mary Dozier and Catherine Ayers in 2021 showed that object attachment exists across our life span, with fluctuations in levels of attachment. For healthy management of possessions, there isn’t one fixed strategy across individuals or even within an individual.

Easily accessed possessions can provide comfort, affirming our preferred self concepts and improving our quality of life. Or they can disrupt our sense of self. The unplayed upright piano in our living room may reinforce our self concept of being musical. Or it may regularly remind us of what we’ve lost. There are no general rules about such possessions. We need to assess their personal value in our own way.

Gracefully, Incrementally Downsizing

Source: Sarah Chai/Pexels

Most of us want to downsize as we get older, even if we find it difficult. How should we approach the management of our possessions?

1) Focus on what to keep, instead of what to throw away. Ask what items matter most or what stories lie behind cherished objects.

2) Begin by clearing out the more obvious, low-emotion areas first, such as the basement, attic, or garage. When considering the living room or bedrooms, we should give ourselves time and many iterations.

3) Before substantially downsizing, seek information and support from peers who have gone through the same thing.

4) Avoid an “Antiques Roadshow” perspective. The potential value of our possessions is not a sound reason for keeping them—unless they are appraised works of art or age-worthy bottles of wine. Chances are, they are not objectively valuable or not easily sold as individual items.

5) Research the cost of companies in the area that manage the clearing out, donating, and selling of belongings. Include that amount in a will for that particular purpose.3

Encouraging Words

Downsizing decisions may be easier than anticipated. My sump pump has broken twice in the past eight years during heavy rain, resulting in two basement floods and two separate clear outs. The first clear out was easy because only my low priority possessions were sitting on the basement floor and damaged. After that, I wanted my basement straightened out as quickly as possible, so I placed my surviving (and more treasured) possessions on the basement floor—which were then damaged eight years later during the second flooding. With the second clear out, I learned quickly I could live without these more treasured items. I don’t recommend flooding, but it could be imagined to allow more ruthless triage on our mostly unused belongings.

item.title: How Shame Can Drive Crime
item.description:
Shame

How Shame Can Drive Crime

Shame may be invisible, but it can lead to destructive acts.

Posted November 9, 2026

Key points
  • Shame is a normal part of life, but excessive shame can create serious problems.
  • Child abuse causes intense shame and devaluation of the self.
  • Unmanageable feelings of shame can lead to aggression and violence.

Shame is often said to be the most powerful emotion. We have all felt the sharp pain of shame: the fear that we are not good enough. “Shame strikes deepest into the heart of man…it is an inner torment, a sickness of the soul…” (Sedgwick & Frank, as cited in George, 2025).

Shaming can—and does—occur every day in parent-child relationships as a means of communicating that a behavior is undesirable or unacceptable, helping children learn social norms. Its inhibitory effect can be protective. Although such moments may be difficult, this kind of corrective shaming is most often followed by a restoration of connection with the parent and reassurance that bad behavior does not define the child as bad or unacceptable.

Effects of Excessive Shame on Children

Early shame expressions have been observed in infants as young as 7 months, and self-awareness emerges in the second year of life (George, 2025), during the phase identified by Erik Erikson as “Autonomy vs. Shame and Doubt.” The central tasks during toddlerhood are learning to do things on one’s own and developing skills, self-control, and self-confidence. When caregivers are overly restrictive, harsh, or critical, the shame that arises can instead lead to self-doubt and low self-esteem.

Serious problems arise when withdrawal of love accompanies shaming, and the “bad” behavior is not differentiated from the person of the child, leading to a more global sense of being flawed or unlovable as a human being. Unbearable feelings of shame can follow. A young child whose parent turns away or conveys contempt or indifference must find a way to manage without the parent’s help. There is no repair to provide relief, reconnection, and the ability to move forward.

Shame is biologically stressful. The flood of painful emotion inhibits speech and thought, and the person feels acutely self-conscious, small, and exposed (Herman, 2018). Children erect defenses to protect themselves from the pain of devaluation of the self. They may become enraged, turning the discomfort of self-blame into blaming others. They may become perfectionistic, hoping that being perfect will protect them from criticism and rejection. They may withdraw from other people, finding safety in isolation.

Child abuse, such as violence or the threat of violence, control of bodily functions, or degradation, subjects children to shame states that are overwhelming. They experience “an intense and destructive sense of self-disgust, verging on self-hatred” when they are treated as a physical object by those who would be expected to love and care for them (Fonagy et al., 2003, as cited in Herman, 2018). These powerful feelings of self-hate do not evaporate and are easily set off by future events.

We know that childhood maltreatment is associated with risk for committing future violence among juveniles and adults. Hypothesized links between violence and childhood abuse include learning violent behavior from parents, effects of trauma on brain development and functioning, including dysregulation of the stress response system and deficits in self-regulation (Miley, Fox, Muniz et al., 2020; Burke, Ellis, Peltier, et al., 2023). There is little in the literature that examines the contribution of the shame that arises from experiences of child abuse, but I believe it is an invisible contributor more often than we think.

How Shame Can Lead to Aggression and Violence

Significant levels of shame can lead to withdrawal or to greater externalizing and aggressive tendencies (Maggi, Zaccaria & Breda et al., 2022). People who suffer pervasive feelings of devaluation and inadequacy fear exposure of the devalued self and mask it with acts of aggression. I saw this in juvenile offenders I interviewed for my book, Before Their Crimes: What We’re Misunderstanding about Childhood Trauma, Youth Crime, and the Path to Healing.

One boy, Simon (not his real name), routinely brutally beaten by his father, was infuriated when some younger members of his gang refused to do his bidding during a confrontation with another gang. “I felt I needed to prove myself, not only to myself, but to the younger guys. I said f*ck it, and I pulled the trigger.” In a moment, his life and that of another boy ended tragically.

Carl (another pseudonym) was physically abused by his mother throughout childhood. The family had modest means, and as a teenager, Carl was intensely ashamed as he compared himself to other kids. He felt compelled to begin stealing to acquire clothes and objects that assuaged a profound sense of inferiority and inadequacy.

A second way that shame is sometimes a factor in aggression and violence is that it impairs the development of the capacity for empathy (Maggi, Zaccaria & Breda et al., 2022). Empathy develops in and through relationships in which we feel seen, heard, and loved. Maltreated children have instead been harshly treated in a context where empathic response is absent.

Most children are unable to manage traumatic experiences or overwhelming shame on their own. Unmanageable feelings must be kept at bay and people at a distance to protect the vulnerable self. If you can’t allow people close to you, there is no chance to develop relationships that might be reparative. When you cannot permit your own feelings, the feelings of others are not real to you. You don’t see your victims as human beings like yourself, but as threats or enemies that must be defeated or destroyed.

When abused children turn to crime, the traumatic nature of maltreatment plays a central role in disrupting normal development. We should not forget that the shame of feeling unlovable and devalued that accompanies abuse compounds the damage and finds its way into the dire strategies meant to protect the shattered sense of self.

item.title: I’m a 70-Year-Old Woman. So What's Ahead?
item.description:
Personal Perspectives

I’m a 70-Year-Old Woman. So What's Ahead?

Personal Perspective: Turning 70 is much more than just a number.

Posted November 9, 2026

Key points
  • Turning 70 can prompt a search for new meaning even when life is healthy, full, and satisfying.
  • Letting go of adult children is an ongoing adjustment, not a single parenting milestone.
  • Gratitude for ordinary family moments can ease uncertainty without resolving it permanently.

I turned 70 in October. My best friend, who is two months older than me, kept telling me it is okay and that once I decide how I’m going to mark the day, my life will get back on track. I knew she was right, but as the weeks approached, I started to think about what 70 meant for me. None of the other decades had hit me in this way.

Is this moment a reminder? An opportunity to think about how to make meaning and how I want to live my life from now? Do I want change?

I wondered why I was reflecting on this, anyway. I figured that by thinking about it intentionally (that new overused word that I love) it must mean that there is some sort of change happening. An awareness of another passing.

So what’s my new game plan?

I'm taking emotional stock of where I am.

I have a full life with my husband of 48 years, and we are both healthy. Big tick.

I have three children who are all partnered, settled, and have worthwhile creative lives. I have five beautiful grandchildren, from 15 to almost 3, and another due next year. They light up my life, and I love spending time with them. They are growing up quickly. Even the 3-year-old already has a full calendar.

I have friends and family in Australia and in the U.S.

I have a satisfying work life.

All ticks.

So the question is, why would I want to change anything?

That's the rational answer.

But something was still unsettling me.

Then I realised that I was on the precipice of a new phase of letting go. My playbook, guided by the work of Edna Furman, to let go of my children at each stage holds, and I know at 70 I have yet a new bridge to cross. A vital one.

But what is this bridge? My children don't need me on a day-to-day basis; they are all separate, self-sufficient, and inhabit their own orbits.

Seventy is a recalibration. There is a sort of tussle with my own and my husband’s mortality. Not in a morbid way, but in a real way that I hadn’t thought about before.

It's a recognition that while we are okay now, a time will come when we go to the doctor and… I am constantly aware that many other people, including those much younger than us, must manage this reality daily.

I go back 12 years to when I single-handedly took my twin grandchildren to the park and chased them both as they went in different directions. I am very active, but could I do this now? I have trouble safely keeping up with a 3-year-old running down the street.

I need to reconsider how to find my new meaning. I turn to role models, those women who are the same stage as me. I find comfort once again in the words of my best friend, who has been a major part of my life for 58 years. She is also in the process of letting go of her children; we have talked about it incessantly for the last 10 years. While she has three daughters that she is very close to, and is available when really needed, she made the intentional decision not to be “the sleepover Nanna." Her artwork nourishes her, as does her time with her family. She refuses to rush, and she has found peace. Most of the time.

I think about how this can apply to me. I know I’d like to read more because it feeds my soul. I have a particular volunteer programme that I am going to embark on.

And I want to continue my work on letting go, mothering, and maybe some literature and film. I’m not sure yet.

The reality is my disquiet will lead me somewhere. It always does.

Reality Check

As always, I go to psychological theory to help me.

The words of Edna Furman come rushing back into my mind. They have guided me to let go, that others are "there to be left." I am faced with yet another new adjustment. The post I wrote last April needs an update.

Then I go to respected psychoanalyst Erik Erikson, whose developmental life stages offer guidance for psychosocial growth. He presents life clearly as a struggle between major turning points which need to be resolved before moving forward. According to this, I’m moving from middle adulthood, generativity vs. stagnation, toward later adulthood, which occurs at 65-plus, marked by integrity vs. despair.

How does this apply to me? I take this as my need to be generative, productive, and useful, while I move toward wisdom and fighting off the negativity about mortality and decline. I recall the mantras that I repeat daily: don't be a victim, no shoulds, it’s not about me, adapt and harness positive energy.

Then I imagine what journalist Abigail Shrier, in her “Tough Love” advice column in Free Press, would say to me in her loving, chiding way.

Gratitude

And just today I got the biggest reminder, which I’m going to bottle.

It’s about gratitude.

My daughter is spending the day with me as we both sit on the couch, do some writing, eat doughnuts, and laugh together.

Then my son drops in to do a call and comes into the kitchen and gives me a warm hug.

Then my other son texts me. Do you want tickets for a show tonight?

I feel so full and back on track for today.

Tomorrow I will be struggling again, but that’s okay.

In Abigail’s words: Onward.

item.title: Hidden Behind the Badge
item.description:
Stress

Hidden Behind the Badge

Exploring stress and burnout among women in law enforcement.

Posted November 9, 2026

Key points
  • Female officers face unique and often overlooked stressors.
  • Organizational culture creates barriers to help-seeking.
  • The consequences of not seeking help are significant and potentially life-threatening.
  • Gender-specific wellness programs are essential.

Co-authored by Dr. Jessica Muccione and Dr. Michael Pittaro

Every occupation can take a toll on workers’ mental health, but some professions are considered more stressful than others due to the nature of work-related exposures. To date, policing remains one of the most stressful professions. Hidden behind every badge is a law enforcement professional trying their very best to navigate a steady, and at times relentless, stream of psychological and emotional stress that makes resilience a key attribute that is essential for survival where suicide rates exceed those of the average citizen. Most, if not all, law enforcement officers will, at some point in their careers, be faced with stressful, traumatic encounters that quite literally become embedded in their psyche, and if not addressed, will likely worsen.

Police Vehicles
Source: Martin Podsied / Unsplash

This topic has been extensively studied, but most studies focus exclusively on male police officers; yet, emerging research suggests that female officers, in particular, often experience these challenges in distinct and deeply personal ways that differ from the experiences of male officers. Exploring these differences can help agencies design wellness initiatives that truly support all who serve by recognizing and adjusting for gender differences. Although the percentage of female officers pursuing a career in law enforcement has been steadily increasing, female officers only comprise 13.8% of all US law enforcement officers; that is likely why their unique circumstances have been largely understudied and, for the most part, overlooked within the research and practitioner literature (Statista, 2024).

Law enforcement officers are repeatedly exposed to traumatic incidents, most of which are attributed to operational stress. Operational stress is commonly tied to the trauma that police officers encounter in the course of their work, such as responding to homicide scenes, domestic and sexual assaults, fatal collisions, suicides, and other acts of violence that can have a profound influence on officers, leading to anxiety, depression, sleep disturbances, PTSD, and in some extreme cases, suicide (Bishopp et al., 2019). To compound matters, today’s law enforcement officers are also faced with staff shortages, mandatory overtime, erratic shifts, insufficient pay, public scrutiny, and at times, unsupportive, ineffective leadership. In fact, Violanti et al. (2017) found that female police officers report a roughly 37% higher prevalence of lack of support from supervisors compared to male officers.

Officers talking
Source: Erik Mclean / Unsplash

The paucity of research to date suggests that female officers are more likely to internalize the emotional impact of stressors that lead to burnout when compared to male officers (Rabichuk, Williamson, & Frankel, 2025). In law enforcement, female officers often place significant pressure on themselves. There is a constant burden to maintain a professional image and avoid appearing vulnerable or weak. In response, female officers tend to suppress emotions rather than seek help because they are persistently compelled to prove their competence in a historically male-dominated field, contributing to the high likelihood of chronic stress and burnout.

Female officers are challenged with unique workplace stressors that extend beyond the basic demands of police work, some of which male officers cannot relate to, and as a result, can adversely affect performance, well-being, retention, and career advancement. Some of these stressors include, but are not limited to, pregnancy, postpartum recovery, menopause, and the demands of shift work. It should come as no surprise that contemporary research suggests that police leaders who understand these realities are better positioned to implement policies that support female officer wellness while strengthening organizational effectiveness.

NYPD Female Officer
Source: Olek Buzunov / Unsplash

Pregnancy and Maternal Health Challenges in Policing

Pregnancy presents unique challenges for women in law enforcement, particularly when agency policies regarding modified assignments and accommodations vary widely. Research suggests female officers may experience elevated reproductive health risks, including miscarriage, highlighting the need for evidence-based workplace policies, reproductive health education, flexible assignments, and supportive supervision.

Postpartum Recovery and the Transition Back to Duty

Illias, Demou, and Riach (2025) emphasized that returning to work after childbirth presents another set of challenges unique to female law enforcement officers. Recovery from childbirth, sleep disruptions, breastfeeding, and childcare responsibilities often lead to concerns about job security and future career advancement. Female officers who received little to no agency support upon return to work experienced significantly higher rates of depression and anxiety than those who had the support of their agencies (Illias et al., 2025). It is therefore recommended that police leaders create family-friendly policies, comprehensive return-to-work policies and programs, breastfeeding spaces, and other supportive accommodations.

Menopause: The Last Workplace Taboo

This is undoubtedly one of the least studied issues affecting female police officers. Hofman and Spiegel (2026) conducted a qualitative study in which the study’s participants (female police officers) reported concerns about stigma, perceptions of reduced competence, and a lack of understanding from leadership. For police leadership, menopause should be viewed as a workforce wellness issue as opposed to a personal matter (Hofman & Spiegel, 2026). Educating and training supervisors and fellow officers normalizes conversations about women’s health that are typically shunned.

Understanding the realities that female officers face throughout their policing careers is not simply a gender-equity issue, but rather an organizational issue because agencies that recognize and respond to these challenges are more likely than not to retain female officers, improve wellness outcomes, and strengthen modern-day law enforcement agencies.

Dr. Jessica Muccione began her law enforcement career in 2016 in Luzerne County, Pennsylvania, before transitioning to a police department in Northampton County, Pennsylvania, in 2018, where she continues to serve as a full-time police officer. She is also an instructor at the Lackawanna College Police Academy for MPOETC and an Adjunct Professor in the college’s Cybersecurity Program. Dr. Muccione holds a Ph.D. in Criminal Justice, a Master’s Degree in Criminology, a Bachelor’s Degree in Homeland and International Security, and an Associate’s Degree in Criminal Justice. She has earned professional certificates in Law Enforcement Administrative Development from Walden University and Supervision of Police Personnel from Northwestern University’s School of Police Staff & Command. Her published qualitative research examines the impact of male sexual offender recidivism on sex crime investigations and is available at https://scholarworks.waldenu.edu/dissertations/14367/.

item.title: Reframing How to Manage Gen Z—Could the Problem Be Us?
item.description:
Leadership

Reframing How to Manage Gen Z—Could the Problem Be Us?

We must see Gen Z needs and differences as a signal to reframe our leadership.

Posted November 9, 2026

Key points
  • It is natural to see flaws in young team members and assume it's immaturity.
  • Often, young staff have visibility into the future and can help others reframe their style.
  • Gen Z's contrarian viewpoint can guide a team to evolve and make progress.

In my new book, The Future Begins With Z—I challenge business leaders who report that young employees are the toughest age group to manage. I suggest we reframe the issue: Instead of complaining about their attitudes, unprofessional conduct, and disrespect, we should look for any kernels of truth and foresight into the future. It’s easy for older generations to assume the world is getting worse.

No doubt, there’s a tension at play—but I wonder if we’re solving the wrong problem.

Is Generation Z genuinely difficult to manage, or are they simply less willing to quietly accept workplace norms that previous generations were taught never to question?

Are We Leading Toward the Future or Longing for the Past?

It is easy to describe a generation as demanding or entitled when it asks for more feedback, greater flexibility, meaningful work, attention to mental health, and for leaders to listen. But a more revealing question is why we interpret these expectations as unreasonable rather than as signals that the traditional relationship between employee and employer is shifting.

Caleb would agree. After he graduated college, he went to work for a Fortune 500 company in New York, serving on the business development team. Caleb was a talented 22-year-old who quickly saw ways the company could improve their use of AI, as well as its HR and operational systems. His supervisor, however, wasn’t interested in his ideas and told Caleb to “pay his dues” before he offered any advice. In less than a year, Caleb quit his job and has since launched three businesses of his own. He’s now leading one that leverages AI to get work done more efficiently. I believe his first boss missed out on an incredible talent.

Nicki would agree. She was 21 years old when her supervisor exposed how little he knew about his young team member. He accused her of having a poor work ethic, since she never worked a minute past 5:00 pm. She had to explain that she left at 5:00 to rush over to a side hustle, since her salary wasn’t enough to pay the bills. (She worked another side hustle on weekends as well.) Like Caleb, Nicki left the company. This turnover will continue to happen until older managers stop stereotyping and get acquainted with their young employees.

Ashton would agree. He started working as a sixth grader but saw jobs differently than his much older boss. This 11-year-old left behind a structured lawn company to start his own business after noticing his neighbors struggling with dirty trash bins. He wondered: Would someone pay to have them cleaned? He discovered they would. Within months, Ashton’s new company was earning him a high income to put in savings, and his work went viral on TikTok, showing how a young leader solving a local problem can inspire everyone.

Reframing the Issue Could Save Us All

Reframing this issue has helped so many organizations I have served. Rather than treating Gen Z as a workplace problem to solve, I ask leaders to consider what this generation might be revealing about the future of work.

Let me offer six questions to ask yourself if you’ve experienced clashes with younger teammates and have assumed they need to do all the changing:

  1. Could their contrary point of view be revealing insight that requires your company to evolve, but it comes disguised as immaturity?
  2. Is their conduct shedding light on today’s cultural shift away from authority-based leadership and toward trust-based connections between boss and staff?
  3. When they want to offer input or feedback, do you try to avoid it, or do you welcome their input as a glimpse into the future of the workplace?
  4. Can their opinions provide foresight into tomorrow’s customers’ mindset and values, instead of merely a childish, inexperienced opinion?
  5. Is it possible that young staff who leverage AI, robotics, and different tech habits aren't necessarily demonstrating a lack of work ethic?
  6. Could the dialogue they want with you be a source of genuine progress, instead of an interruption in your day?

Perhaps it’s time we seek growth over comfort and familiarity. If we do, however, it will require intentionality. I’m in Orlando today, spending time with my new grandson, Max. He’s 9 weeks old. When he’s awake, he constantly fidgets and groans, making sweet little noises and movements. Doctors say babies often do this in search of comfort. Each move is a search for comfort for their bodies or food if they’re hungry. This is a natural urge humans have all our lives—to find comfort and satisfaction. Call it "the comfort zone."

Leaders, however, must resist this natural quest for comfort and seek growth and progress. In our day, I believe this means learning from our young instead of just lecturing them. Let’s reframe how we perceive our youngest teammates. Maybe, just maybe, they’ll lead us into a better future.
